passages.t: Baruch writes the scroll and reads it in the temple
passages.happening:
In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, God tells Jeremiah to take a scroll and write on it all the words he has spoken to him since the days of Josiah (verses 1 and 2). ‘Perhaps when the people of Judah hear about all the calamity I plan to bring upon them, each of them will turn from his wicked way. Then I will forgive their iniquity and their sin’ (verse 3).

Jeremiah calls Baruch son of Neriah, and Baruch writes on the scroll at Jeremiah's dictation (verse 4). Jeremiah is barred from the LORD's house, so he sends Baruch to read the scroll there on a fast day (verses 5 and 6), hoping the people will plead with God and turn (verse 7).

In the ninth month of the fifth year, a fast is called (verse 9). Baruch reads the scroll from the room of Gemariah son of Shaphan in the upper court, at the New Gate (verse 10). Gemariah's son Micaiah hears it and goes down to tell the officials in the palace (verses 11 to 13). They send for Baruch and have him read it to them (verses 14 and 15). They turn to one another in fear and say they must report it all to the king (verse 16). They ask how he wrote it, and he says at Jeremiah's dictation, in ink (verses 17 and 18). They tell Baruch that he and Jeremiah must hide (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The fourth year of Jehoiakim is 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar defeated Egypt at Carchemish and became the great power of the region. The reading came in the winter of 604 BC. With Babylon's army on the move, a public fast was called.

Several of the officials belong to one family. Shaphan was the royal scribe who read the rediscovered book of the law to King Josiah. His son Ahikam protected Jeremiah in chapter 26. His son Gemariah lent his room for this reading, and his grandson Micaiah carried the news. They feared the word and protected the messengers.

The chapter shows how part of the book of Jeremiah came to be written. The prophet spoke, and a scribe wrote. God's reason for the scroll is in verse 3: perhaps they will turn, and he will forgive.
passages.later: When Josiah heard the book of the law read, ‘he tore his clothes’ (2 Kings 22:11). The same family of Shaphan had served Josiah and now protected Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24).
passages.asks: The officials heard the scroll and were afraid, and they protected those who wrote it. Ask how you respond when God's word unsettles you. And ask whom you could protect who is bringing a hard but true message.

passages.t: The king burns the scroll, and it is written again
passages.happening:
The officials leave the scroll in the room of Elishama the scribe and go to the king (verse 20). He sends Jehudi to fetch it, and Jehudi reads it to the king and all the officials standing beside him (verse 21). It is the ninth month, and the king sits in his winter house with a fire burning in the firepot before him (verse 22).

‘And as soon as Jehudi had read three or four columns, Jehoiakim would cut them off with a scribe’s knife and throw them into the firepot, until the entire scroll had been consumed by the fire’ (verse 23). ‘Yet in hearing all these words, the king and his servants did not become frightened or tear their garments’ (verse 24). Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah begged him not to burn it, but he would not listen (verse 25). He ordered Baruch and Jeremiah arrested, ‘but the LORD had hidden them’ (verse 26).

God tells Jeremiah to take another scroll and write all the words again (verse 28). Jehoiakim will have no one to sit on David's throne, and his body will be thrown out to the heat by day and frost by night (verse 30). Jeremiah gives another scroll to Baruch, who writes all the words of the burned scroll, ‘And many similar words were added to them’ (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Scrolls were written in columns on sheets sewn together. The king cut off each section as it was read and burned it, column by column, a deliberate public contempt. His servants did not tear their clothes, the usual sign of grief and repentance. Their grandfather's generation had done exactly that when Josiah heard the law.

The word survived the fire. The second scroll held everything from the first and more besides. The book of Jeremiah itself grew from that second scroll.

The judgment on Jehoiakim repeats 22:19. His son Jehoiachin did reign briefly, for three months, before he was taken to Babylon.
passages.later: Isaiah says, ‘The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever’ (Isaiah 40:8). The same Elnathan who begged the king had once fetched the prophet Uriah back from Egypt (Jeremiah 26:22).
passages.hard:
Jeremiah says Jehoiakim will have no one on David's throne and his body will be thrown out, but his son Jehoiachin did reign, and 2 Kings says Jehoiakim rested with his fathers. How do these fit?

The difficulty is real. Jehoiachin succeeded his father but reigned only three months before Nebuchadnezzar took him to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:8-15), and 22:30 says none of his offspring would sit on the throne. Many interpreters read no one to sit on David's throne as no lasting successor, no line that continued through him, which is what happened. On the body, 2 Kings uses the common formula of resting with one's fathers, which marks a death without necessarily describing a burial, and it does not say where he was buried. Some think his body was dishonored during the Babylonian advance of 598 or 597 BC; others read Jeremiah's words, here and in 22:19, as judgment in the stock language of dishonor. Scripture does not settle it.
passages.asks: The king cut up God's word and burned it, and the word came back larger. Ask which parts of God's word you would rather cut out. And ask what it means for you that no fire has been able to silence it.
